answer.label: Not Edgar Allan Poe — a 21st-century Twitter line
answer.authorDates: Tweet of 9 November 2011, per Quote Investigator
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ found this line in none of Poe’s stories or essays. It traces the popular wording to a 9 November 2011 tweet by the social-media persona @Edgar_Allan_Poe, which it calls “probably the origin”; Poe died in 1849.

source.excerpt: The scariest monsters are the ones that lurk within our souls.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ reports it has not found the expression in Poe’s stories or essays, and concludes: “The statement was constructed long after the death of Poe.”
The same QI article ↗ identifies a 9 November 2011 tweet by the persona @Edgar_Allan_Poe as “the primary locus of popularization for the quote and probably the origin.”

QI also notes a similar thought decades earlier, in a 28 December 1982 New York Times review of the TV film Mazes and Monsters: “The most frightening monsters are the ones that exist in our minds” (QI ↗).
Wikiquote’s Edgar Allan Poe page ↗ does not include the line in any section (checked 3 November 2026).
source.excerptNote: The wording as Quote Investigator transcribes it from the 9 November 2011 @Edgar_Allan_Poe tweet. No version of this sentence appears in any Poe text QI examined.

author.name: Edgar Allan Poe
author.heading: The writer it gets pinned on
author.bio: Poe was the American master of the macabre, author of The Raven, The Tell-Tale Heart and The Fall of the House of Usher. His tales of guilt and self-destruction make him a natural magnet for lines about “inner monsters” — but this sentence is not in his writings; it surfaced on Twitter more than 160 years after his death.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Poe
misattribution.intro: Poe is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for invented quotations, and a dark line about inner monsters sounds like him. A Twitter account posting in his name made the pairing look official.

items.scope: Quote sites, image macros, social media
items.why: Quote collections credit the line to Poe without a source. Quote Investigator ↗ found it in none of his stories or essays and traces it to a 9 November 2011 tweet by the @Edgar_Allan_Poe persona — an account using Poe’s name, not Poe himself, who died in 1849.

misattribution.truthLine: No Poe text contains this sentence. Its probable origin is a 2011 tweet by a Poe-persona Twitter account, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it feels like Poe
lead: The idea that the real horror lives inside us runs through Poe’s fiction — narrators undone by their own guilt and compulsions. That resemblance is what makes the line believable, but resemblance is not authorship: the sentence itself first shows up on Twitter, not in any of his tales, poems or essays.
A Twitter account that writes in a famous author’s voice can launch a “quote” that is then copied without the account name, leaving only the author’s. Quote Investigator’s finding fits that pattern.
context.pull: The statement was constructed long after the death of Poe. — Quote Investigator
